overview:
Apramatta‑samyata (अप्रमत्त‑संयत / अप्पमत्त‑संयत) is a classical Jain term describing the state of being a **vigilant, fully attentive, and unwaveringly disciplined practitioner** of samyata—ethical restraint. In both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions, it is treated as a technical category within the broader analysis of conduct (cāritra), right path (mārga), and the progression through the guṇasthānas.

The term combines *apramatta* (“not negligent, free from carelessness”) and *samyata* (“one who has adopted restraint”). Thus, apramatta‑samyata refers to a practitioner—monastic or lay—who has embraced restraint and practices it **without lapses**, maintaining continuous mindfulness of vows, bodily actions, speech, and mental states. In the guṇasthāna system, apramatta‑samyata is associated with the **seventh guṇasthāna**, where the aspirant has overcome pramāda (negligence) and practices samyama with heightened vigilance.

Classical sources describe pramāda as a subtle inner dullness arising from passions, inattentiveness, or laxity. Apramatta‑samyata is therefore not merely ethical behavior but a **psychological and spiritual condition** in which vigilance becomes stable. Commentaries emphasize that this state is essential for progressing toward higher guṇasthānas, where passions are progressively attenuated and right conduct becomes increasingly spontaneous.

Across traditions, apramatta‑samyata is treated as a **technical milestone**, not a status conferred by any living authority. It is defined by canonical criteria: absence of negligence, stable restraint, and continuous awareness. Modern scholarship highlights its role in Jain moral psychology, showing how it bridges ethical discipline and meditative attentiveness.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.15
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.translation: “One who is free from negligence is restrained.”
primary_sources.notes: This sutra is the most frequently cited canonical definition. Both Digambara and Śvetāmbara commentaries agree that apramatta‑samyata marks the seventh guṇasthāna, where restraint is practiced without pramāda (negligence).

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra 9.1–9.2 (contextual)
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.notes: These lines elaborate the psychological basis of pramāda and its removal. They clarify why apramatta‑samyata is considered a purified form of samyata.

primary_sources.title: Gommatasāra (Cāritra‑kāṇḍa) 7.1–7.4
primary_sources.author: Nemichandra Siddhānta‑cakravartin
primary_sources.notes: Digambara analysis provides detailed criteria for apramatta‑samyata, linking it to the attenuation of passions and continuous vigilance in conduct.

primary_sources.title: Daśavaikālika Sūtra 4.1 (Śvetāmbara)
primary_sources.author: Traditional attribution to the early canonical compilers
primary_sources.notes: Although not a technical definition, this passage is used in Śvetāmbara commentaries to illustrate the ideal of apramāda as foundational to samyata.

misconceptions.myth: Apramatta‑samyata refers to a special monastic rank or title granted by a living teacher.
misconceptions.reality: Classical texts define apramatta‑samyata as a **state of conduct and vigilance**, not a title. It is a doctrinal category within the guṇasthāna system and does not depend on institutional recognition.
It indicates **absence of negligence**, not total eradication of passions. Passions are significantly reduced but not fully eliminated until higher guṇasthānas.

Primary texts describe apramatta‑samyata as a technical state of restraint. While traditionally associated with monastic discipline, the conceptual framework applies to any practitioner analyzing conduct through the guṇasthāna model.
